cause: The rule catches common verbs (see, look, think, feel, indicate, speak) in completely normal uses: legal boilerplate disclaimers ('The content speaks only as of the date indicated', 'should not be relied upon'), literal physical instructions ('focus on the road'), noun forms counted as verbs ('perception of Silicon Valley'), and quoted interview speech. A single a16z disclaimer template fires 20+ times in the 30 samples. No sample in this set is sloppy writing.

For fitness, medical, sports, and travel content this is expected and domain-correct: exercise instructions must name muscles and movements, walking/running comparisons must reference physical actions, and medical anatomy descriptions require body-part vocabulary. The non-fitness samples (paulgraham, a16z) are mostly truncated 10-20 word fragments where context is insufficient to judge density meaningfully.

cause: The rule flags passages dense with 'weak' body/action beats (is, has, helps, creates, looks, comes). Gov/health text (MedlinePlus-style patient education) legitimately uses plain simple-verb sentences for accessibility. RFC protocol definitions use 'is', 'can', 'needs', 'provides' as precise technical copulas. Victorian fiction narrates sequential physical actions in plot. Paul Graham samples are 15-word truncated fragments with no usable context. None represent sloppy writing.

cause: The rule fires on any simple action verb ('stood', 'remained', 'followed', 'looked') framed as a 'placeholding beat'. Wikipedia biographical prose uses these verbs as precise factual statements of what a person did. Victorian fiction uses them as literal scene narration. The Keats poem line 'She stood in tears amid the alien corn' is canonical poetry. The food/stackexchange entry narrates a controlled culinary experiment where each action verb is a distinct procedural step. None are padding.
